analysis.one_liner: Exempts farm animal-waste air emissions from federal toxic-release reporting rules.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to spare farms from reporting ammonia and other hazardous air emissions drew 39 Senate cosponsors and a subcommittee hearing, but never reached a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires anyone releasing certain hazardous substances to notify officials, so the public and emergency responders know about them. After a court ruling, air emissions from animal waste at farms were set to be covered by that rule. This bill would permanently exempt those emissions — ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, and gases from manure — from the reporting, recordkeeping, and penalty requirements, and would exempt the handling and storage of registered pesticides too. It got a hearing but never a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Large livestock, poultry, and fish operations, whose manure releases hazardous gases. Without the exemption, they would have to report emissions to federal and state responders, and those reports become public. The bill would lift that paperwork and the public notice.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes air emissions from animal waste at farms — including decomposing waste mixed with bedding, feed, or compost — from CERCLA's release notification, recordkeeping, and penalty requirements.
It also removes the application, handling, and storage of federally registered pesticides at farms from those same requirements.
The bill leaves in place every other part of the Superfund law, including cleanup authority, so it narrows only the notice requirement.

analysis.who_pays: People living near large livestock operations would lose public notice when farms release hazardous gases, and emergency responders would lose data they could use. The cost is information, not money.

drawbacks.text: The bill would end public reporting of ammonia and hydrogen sulfide emissions from animal waste, so neighbors and state officials would no longer learn about these releases through the federal system.

The exemption is written to cover any farm producing at least $1,000 of agricultural products a year, so it reaches far beyond small family farms and shelters the largest operations from the disclosure rule.

An honest supporter would note the exemption is disclosure-only — it preserves cleanup liability — but removing the reports also removes the public record that communities could use to press for cleaner practices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The industry's case was that a court decision had turned a paperwork rule into a burden reaching many ordinary farms reporting trivial emissions. But the bill, as written, goes further: its $1,000 farm-year threshold exempts operations of nearly any size, and what is lost is not just paperwork but the public record of hazardous emissions near rural communities. The exemption would be permanent, while the burden it addressed could have been tailored.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate environment committee, got one subcommittee hearing, and then sat there until the Congress ended with no committee vote and no floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill would exempt air emissions from animal waste at farms from the Superfund law's release notification, recordkeeping, and penalty requirements.
It would also exempt the handling and storage of registered pesticide products by agricultural producers from those requirements.
It was introduced on February 13, 2018 with 21 original cosponsors from both parties, and drew 39 cosponsors in total: 15 Democrats and 24 Republicans.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, whose Superfund subcommittee held a hearing on March 8, 2018.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Livestock and poultry operations were better off with the bill dead, because reporting had already been delayed by regulators, and without a law there was still a chance to craft an exemption that spared small farms rather than all of them. Neighbors of large farms kept the legal framework that entitles communities to notice of hazardous releases.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Rural neighbors, at least for now

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split 24 Republicans and 15 Democrats out of 39 total, making this one of the more bipartisan farm bills of the Congress — yet neither party's leadership brought it to a vote.

industries.note: The bill would permanently spare these operations from reporting ammonia and hydrogen sulfide emissions from manure, and from penalties for failing to report. Their gain comes directly out of the public's right to know what is being released near their homes.

industries.industry: Pesticide manufacturers and agricultural pesticide users
industries.note: The bill also exempts the application, handling, and storage of registered pesticides at farms from release reporting and penalties, closing off a disclosure path for agricultural chemical releases.

industries.industry: Emergency responders and state environmental agencies
industries.note: They would lose the release reports they use to know what hazardous substances are present at a site before responding or enforcing.
